clue: Where does Japan's tallest and most sacred mountain stand?
fact: This symmetrical volcano last erupted in 1707 and has been climbed as a pilgrimage for centuries.

clue: Where is Africa's tallest mountain?
fact: This free-standing volcanic massif in Tanzania rises straight from savanna plains to a snow-capped summit at 5,895 meters.

clue: Where do giant stone moai statues stand watch over the ocean?
fact: The Rapa Nui people carved nearly 900 moai between the 13th and 16th centuries on this remote volcanic island.

clue: Where does a tidal island crowned by an abbey rise from the sea?
fact: At high tide this Normandy island is cut off from the mainland, with waters that can rush in faster than a person can run.

clue: Where does the fairy-tale castle that inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle stand?
fact: Bavarian King Ludwig II built it in the 1860s as a private retreat and never saw it finished before his death.

clue: Where do over a million wildebeest migrate across open grassland each year?
fact: This Tanzanian ecosystem hosts the largest terrestrial mammal migration on Earth, a circuit covering roughly 1,000 kilometers.

clue: Where did a young naturalist's finch observations help inspire the theory of evolution?
fact: Charles Darwin visited this volcanic archipelago in 1835, and its isolated wildlife shaped his thinking on natural selection.

clue: Where is a lake so salty that swimmers float effortlessly on its surface?
fact: At roughly 430 meters below sea level, its shore is the lowest point on dry land on Earth.

clue: Where does a building that has served as both a cathedral and a mosque stand?
fact: Completed in 537 AD as a Byzantine cathedral, it held the record for the world's largest interior space for nearly a thousand years.

clue: Where were thousands of life-sized clay soldiers buried to guard an emperor's tomb?
fact: Farmers digging a well in 1974 stumbled on this army of over 8,000 unique terracotta warriors near Xi'an, China.

clue: Where does the world's largest salt flat turn into a giant mirror after rain?
fact: This Bolivian flat covers over 10,000 square kilometers and holds roughly half the world's known lithium reserves.

clue: Where were eleven churches carved downward out of solid volcanic rock?
fact: According to tradition, Ethiopia's King Lalibela ordered them built in the 12th century after a vision of Jerusalem.

clue: Where do hot air balloons drift over valleys of cone-shaped 'fairy chimney' rock formations?
fact: Early Christians carved entire underground cities and cave churches into this soft volcanic rock in central Turkey.

clue: Where do a chain of turquoise lakes cascade over travertine waterfalls?
fact: This Croatian national park's 16 terraced lakes are colored by minerals and shift shade with the light and season.

clue: Where did a legendary trans-Saharan trading city become synonymous with remoteness?
fact: This Malian city flourished in the 14th century as a center of gold, salt, and Islamic scholarship, home to thousands of ancient manuscripts.

clue: Where do alien-looking dragon's blood trees grow on an isolated island?
fact: Isolated for millions of years in the Arabian Sea, this Yemeni island has a third of its plant species found nowhere else on Earth.

clue: Where do white mineral terraces cascade down a hillside like frozen waterfalls?
fact: Calcium-rich hot springs have built up these white travertine terraces in Turkey over thousands of years.

clue: Where is one of the hottest and lowest places on Earth, dotted with sulfur springs and lava lakes?
fact: This Ethiopian desert basin sits over 100 meters below sea level and includes Erta Ale, one of the few volcanoes with a permanent lava lake.

clue: Where does a red-sand desert of towering sandstone cliffs evoke a landscape from Mars?
fact: Nicknamed the 'Valley of the Moon,' this desert has stood in for Mars in several Hollywood films.

clue: Where does a giant bullseye-shaped rock formation visible from space sit in the Sahara?
fact: Nicknamed the 'Eye of the Sahara,' this Mauritanian formation is roughly 40 kilometers wide and was long mistaken for a meteorite impact.

clue: Where is the most remote inhabited island in the world?
fact: This South Atlantic island's main settlement, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, lies about 2,400 kilometers from the nearest other inhabited land.

clue: Where is the point in the ocean farthest from any land?
fact: Named after Jules Verne's submarine captain, this spot in the South Pacific is so remote that astronauts in orbit are sometimes the closest humans to it.

clue: Where is the deepest known point in all of Earth's oceans?
fact: At nearly 11,000 meters down in the Mariana Trench, the pressure here is over 1,000 times that at the ocean's surface.

clue: Where is the largest research station on the coldest continent?
fact: This US Antarctic base sits on volcanic rock and can swell to over 1,000 people in the austral summer.

clue: Where was the coldest temperature ever recorded on Earth's surface?
fact: This Russian station recorded -89.2°C in 1983 and sits atop nearly 4 kilometers of Antarctic ice covering a hidden freshwater lake.

clue: Where did the mutineers of HMS Bounty hide from the Royal Navy?
fact: This tiny Pacific island's roughly 40 residents are mostly descended from the 1789 Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian companions.

clue: Where is the northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth?
fact: This Canadian Forces station sits just 817 kilometers from the North Pole, closer to Russia's coast than to most of Canada.

clue: Where is the highest permanent human settlement on Earth?
fact: This Peruvian gold-mining town sits above 5,100 meters in the Andes, where the air holds about half the oxygen found at sea level.

clue: Where is the most remote island on the planet, uninhabited and almost entirely covered by a glacier?
fact: This Norwegian volcanic island in the South Atlantic lies over 1,600 kilometers from the nearest land, Antarctica.

clue: Where does a palace of twenty-four emperors stand behind a wide moat in China's capital?
fact: Ming and Qing emperors lived inside these walls from 1420 to 1924, and the surviving complex still covers 72 hectares across some 980 buildings.

clue: Where did Ottoman sultans rule for four centuries behind walls above the Bosphorus?
fact: From these ramparts the Janissaries' bodies were flung onto the city below, and the palace harem keeps relics said to have belonged to the Prophet Muhammad.

clue: Where does the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty change guards twice a day in full period costume?
fact: Rebuilt in 1865 after the first palace burned down, its changing of the guard ceremony still recreates the 15th-century ritual of the Joseon kings.

clue: Where does the world's highest mountain pierce the sky?
fact: At 8,849 m Everest is the Nepal-China border peak, and because of the border dispute Nepal's own maps show it as 8,586 m, which makes the country's highest peak the world's 14th.

clue: Where does the largest Buddhist temple in the world climb a volcanic hill in Java?
fact: Built in the 8th-9th century, it wraps 2,672 relief panels around nine stacked platforms, and work stopped in 1006 when the volcano erupted and buried the site.

clue: Where does a 71 m Buddha carved from a cliff watch three rivers meet?
fact: Cut between 1001 and 1153, the figure is so large that a Song emperor once considered damming the river to drown it, and it still holds its own stone umbrella against the weather.

clue: Where do 1,600 limestone towers rise sheer out of the sea?
fact: Marine paleontologists once proposed pouring fossil fuel into these caves to date the world's oldest tropical limestone, and no one has found a better explanation for the karsts' odd chemistry.

clue: Where does a hilltop palace above Jaipur mirror 2,000 pieces of cut glass?
fact: Amber Fort was built with one of the world's earliest formal gardens, laid out in the same nine-square pattern as the planned city that grew below it.

clue: Where do thousands of vermilion torii gates tunnel up a hillside in Kyoto?
fact: Every gate is a donation from a Japanese company, which is why the tunnels never end, and the shrines at the summit are said to grant prosperity in trading.

clue: Where do three grand madrasas frame the great public square of Samarkand?
fact: The square's buildings date from the 1400s to the 1600s, and beside it stood Ulugh Beg's observatory, which measured the length of the year to within a second.

clue: Where do 500 painted caves hold 45 km of Buddhist murals in a desert cliff?
fact: The caves were sealed for a thousand years when sand blew into the library cave, which preserved tens of thousands of scroll paintings dry.

clue: Where do the Dalai Lamas' thirteen-storey winter palace rise above Lhasa at 3,700 m?
fact: The palace was fired in 1959 and rebuilt from the walls that survived, while thousands of monks and nuns had already been expelled from the city.

clue: Where is the highest mountain in Southeast Asia?
fact: At 4,095 m Kinabalu's bare granite summit sits on a still-uplifting fault block, and glaciers that once covered it have been gone since the last ice age.

clue: Where is a fifth-century royal citadel carved into a 200 m rock, guarded by a monumental lion gateway?
fact: The Lion Rock's terraces hold a fresco of a 'cloud woman' nearly identical to one painted at an Indian temple, and the two designs are thought to share a single source.

clue: Where did over 2,000 Buddhist temples once stand on a single plain?
fact: The temples of Bagan were built between 1001 and 1287 on money raised by 10,000 donor inscriptions carved into the sandalwood slabs now kept in museums.

clue: Where has a desert gas fire been burning for half a century?
fact: Soviet geologists lit this natural gas well alight in 1971 expecting it to burn out in weeks; the crater is a 70 m pit of flame that has never gone out.

clue: Where does a Gobi ridge of red cliffs glow like fire at sunset?
fact: The orange sandstone of Bayanzag burned red at dusk long before it was named, and dinosaur skeletons excavated in the 1920s made the site famous for fossils as well.

clue: Where is the second-longest alpine lake in the world, which never freezes?
fact: At 6,248 m in the Kyrgyz Tien Shan, it holds more water by volume than Lake Baikal and was drained by a pre-Catalan-era king who was afraid of the water spirits.

clue: Where were monumental T-shaped stone pillars carved more than 11,000 years ago?
fact: Hunter-gatherers, not farmers, raised this hilltop of enclosures around 9600 BC, which upset the idea that settled agriculture had to come first, and the site was deliberately buried by hand.

clue: Where is a bricked and bitumen-sealed Great Bath from a city that vanished 4,500 years ago?
fact: The Indus metropolis on this mound was abandoned with no sign of warfare, and its drains were laid so carefully that a thousand years of traffic found no need for repairs.

clue: Where does a stone relief of 23 subject nations still watch an empty royal terrace?
fact: This ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid empire was burned by Alexander in 330 BC, yet its gate, treasury columns and audience-hall stairs survive almost intact.

clue: Where did 10,000 monks study for centuries and coin the decimal zero?
fact: This monastery complex in Bihar ran for 700 years, and Chinese pilgrims who studied here carried its ideas home long before the Arabic al-khwarizmi made 'zero' a term Europe would adopt.

clue: Where did Akbar build a red-sandstone capital and abandon it after fourteen years?
fact: The Mughal emperor left this ghost city when the water ran out, and its Buland Darwaza triumphal gate is still the tallest gateway in the world.

clue: Where is a single stone slab inscribed with 1,400 lines of writing?
fact: Sri Lanka's second ancient capital has the Gal Potha, an 8 m stone 'book' that was struck by lightning and toppled in the 1600s, and its elephants still step out of their own shadows.

clue: Where did the opening shots of the Second Sino-Japanese War get fired in August 1937?
fact: A patrol of Japanese troops was refused entry to this Beijing bridge and a firefight began, and the Chinese still keep the old guardhouse as a memorial to the dead.

clue: Where is the world's largest cave passage, with its own jungle, river and clouds inside?
fact: The largest known cave passage system on Earth lay unexplored until 1991, when a climber squeezed through the entrance hole that a sinkhole in Laos had opened into its roof.

clue: Where was the capital of the Mongol Empire, built with bricks from its own temples?
fact: On the Orkhon River the city of Karakorum was raised from Buddhist sculptures and building material taken from Buddhist monuments, then abandoned after one summer of use.

clue: Where is an Indus city with a signboard older than Sumerian writing?
fact: Dholavira's excavators found a stone signboard of painted jars, a stone water-harvesting ring and a fortification that held for centuries, all on an island in Gujarat's Gulf of Kachchh.

clue: Where did a Gobi cliff yield a tyrannosaur egg nest of 22 intact eggs?
fact: The red rocks of this 'Flaming Wall' have given up dozens of dinosaur fossils since the 1920s, and the site is now closed to everyone but scientists for fear of theft.

clue: Where does the Pamir Highway top out, between Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan?
fact: At 4,655 m this is the highest point on the road from Kashgar to Dushanbe, and in winter the pass is closed entirely as ice cliffs hang over the tarmac.

clue: Where is the walled former capital of Mustang, a kingdom in the Himalayas near Tibet?
fact: This plateau town in Mustang is the old capital of the walled Himalayan kingdom of Lo, whose king married a Chinese princess in 1951 after generations of border hostility.

clue: Where is the world's oldest known port, with a dockyard built of stamped bricks?
fact: This Indus town on Gujarat's coast was among the world's earliest planned cities, and its tidal dockyard is built from bricks stamped with the year they were fired.

clue: Where is a glacial lake so high that legends say the goddess Nanda Devi appeared in it?
fact: In Ladakh's upper Bhagirathi valley the lake sits in a basin around 5,050 m, where pilgrims once walked up to see the reflection of the goddess and the surrounding peaks.

clue: Where does a chain of sandbars, called Rama Setu in Hindu tradition, connect two countries?
fact: The 80 km chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka is described as a natural bridge in the Ramayana, but sonar surveys found no channel deep enough for stone piers.

clue: Where does the Hall of Mirrors gleam in the palace that Louis XIV used to dominate Europe from?
fact: Versailles' Hall of Mirrors has 357 mirrors, and the Seine's water was pumped 13 kilometres by the Machine de Marly so the fountains could run every day.

clue: Where does an ancient domed rotunda with a single oculus open onto the sky?
fact: The Panthe's oculus is one 43-metre hole cut in the dome and the only light the interior gets, so rain falls straight onto the marble floor.

clue: Where does the largest church in the world stand under the tallest dome in Rome?
fact: St Peter's dome rises 136.6 metres, second only to Florence's Duomo, and it took four popes and nearly three centuries to finish.

clue: Where does a landmark Gothic cathedral raise twin spires above the Rhine?
fact: Cologne Cathedral took 632 years to finish, and during the Second World War Allied bombs failed to bring down its twin spires.

clue: Where does the gateway with a four-horse chariot on top mark the start of Berlin's main avenue?
fact: Napoleon marched through the Brandenburg Gate into Berlin in 1806, and the Quadriga on top did not come home until 1958.

clue: Where does a stone fortress still keep its ravens, crown jewels and prison cells?
fact: The Tower of London was a royal palace for four centuries before becoming a prison and armoury, and its ravens are the last of a flock kept since the Wild Men.

clue: Where does the onion-domed cathedral with nine chapels and one bell tower stand on Red Square?
fact: St Basil's was named after a holy fool and not after Basil the Great, and it was built in 1561 to mark the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan.

clue: Where does the Parthenon still guard the marble hill above the ancient city?
fact: The Parthenon's corner columns are 2.4% thicker than the middle ones and lean inward, an optical correction that has kept them looking upright for 2,400 years.

clue: Where does the still-unfinished basilica of spires like honeycombs stand?
fact: Gaudi's Sagrada Familia has been under construction since 1882, and his plaster model of it was photographed from a reconnaissance aeroplane in 1926.

clue: Where can you read the wartime diary of a teenage girl in the room where she wrote it?
fact: Anne Frank's diary survived because Fritz Frank and Gies Huber abandoned papers before they were deported in 1942, and it was not published until 1947.

clue: Where does the neo-Gothic parliament with 691 statues face the Danube?
fact: Budapest's Parliament was sited deliberately across the river from Habsburg Buda so the Hungarian nation would stare back at the emperor's own palace.

clue: Where is the winter palace of the tsars turned museum holding millions of artworks?
fact: The Hermitage grew from the 317 paintings Catherine the Great bought in Dutch auctions, and for decades it had no public entrance at all.

clue: Where did a royal dynasty rule for five hundred years from a castle above the Vistula?
fact: Wawel Castle was the seat of Poland's kings for five centuries, and its dragon on the riverbank breathes real flame at visitors twice a day.

clue: Where does a 42-floor Stalin-era skyscraper, presented as a Soviet gift, dominate the skyline?
fact: The Palace of Culture was sent by Stalin to Poland in 1955 as a gift, its construction materials shipped in from 168 Soviet locations.

clue: Where do thirty baroque statues line the footbridge that linked Prague's two halves?
fact: Charles Bridge was the only crossing of the Vltava for five hundred years, and the crowning saint on it is Saint Wenceslas, the patron of Bohemia.

clue: Where does the 600-year-old clock show where the sun and the moon should be?
fact: Prague's astronomical clock has run since 1410, and its slow zodiac disc turns once for the 365 days of the year it keeps.

clue: Where do you climb the fortified circuit of stone walls around a walled Adriatic republic?
fact: UNESCO's inscription for Dubrovnik calls it a city built and defended over three centuries, and the walls enclose an old town barely 300 metres across.

clue: Where is the Carpathian castle whose name is linked for ever to Dracula?
fact: Bran Castle was raised in 1378 not as a royal seat but as a customs post and garrison guarding the trade route through the Carpathian passes.

clue: Where was the Roman town frozen in ash by a volcano in AD 79?
fact: Pompeii's plaster casts were poured into the cavities left by bodies decomposed in the ash, so figures still frozen mid-stride stand in their shops.

clue: Where does a hill fortress of 50 rooms watch over the rooftops of Mozart's birthplace?
fact: Hohensalzburg was finished in 1077 and never taken by assault; a legend says Salzburg's archbishop ordered all but one of its bells silenced as raving mad.

clue: Where do people still live in cave dwellings trodden out of a tuff cliff?
fact: Matera's cisterns under St Peter's Cave hold a cardinal's hat, a papal tiara and a belt preserved in a single drop of water that has not evaporated since the 1300s.

clue: Where do whitewashed cone-roofed trulli stand wall to wall like a village of beehives?
fact: Alberobello's trulli are built of dry-laid limestone without nails or mortar, and the town council still keeps masons on hand to re-roof them by hand.

clue: Where in Orkney was a Neolithic stone town of a dozen houses deliberately buried and abandoned?
fact: The Ness of Brodgar was dug in the 3100s BC, then walled up and left to rot in the rain, which is why five thousand years of it survive.

clue: Where do forty thousand hexagonal basalt columns step down into the North Atlantic?
fact: The Giant's Causeway's columns are lava joints formed as molten rock cooled some 50 million years ago, and Irish legend says a giant built the road across them to Scotland.

clue: Where can you bathe in milky turquoise geothermal water in the middle of a lava field?
fact: The Blue Lagoon is not a natural spring at all: it is the superheated brine runoff of a geothermal power station, kept hot so the plant's pipes never freeze.

clue: Where does a geyser throw boiling water twenty metres up every few minutes?
fact: Strokkur erupts every five to ten minutes, and beside it the Great Geysir, once the most famous on earth, erupted just once in modern times, for four days in 2018.

clue: Where do icebergs calve off a glacier into a lagoon and drift out to sea within the hour?
fact: Jökulsárlón is fed by an outlet glacier of Vatnajökull, Europe's largest ice cap, and its bergs sink and resurface within sight of the beach.

clue: Where does an arrow-shaped mountain with black stripes rise behind a little red church?
fact: Kirkjufell means misty mountain, and the dark stripes on its flank are stacked layers of basalt lavafalls, frozen like the pages of a book.

clue: Where does a square cliff of rock hang 600 metres above a fjord?
fact: Pulpit Rock is a flat square of bare rock planed smooth by a glacier and abandoned unfinished when the brothers who quarried it realised the stone was worthless.

clue: Where does a lone island with a church bell sit in a glacial lake beneath a cliff-top castle?
fact: Lake Bled has Slovenia's only natural island, and to ring its church bell you must wade across from the shore, which men have done since 1788.

clue: Where is Europe's highest summit, a dormant volcano with two snowy tops?
fact: Elbrus tops out at 5,642 metres and its two summits are joined by a three-kilometre saddle of rubble that only climbers have crossed.

clue: Where does Europe's most powerful waterfall drop into a canyon of spray?
fact: Dettifoss plunges 11 metres in two steps on the Jökulsá river, and in summer the canyon fills with a permanent grey drizzle of mist.

clue: Where does Britain's second-deepest lake hide a monster that a surgeon once photographed?
fact: Loch Ness reaches 227 metres in depth, and the 1934 photograph of a flipper that started the modern monster legend is now widely thought to be a duck.

clue: Where do two tectonic plates pull apart at the site of one of the world’s oldest parliaments?
fact: Thingvellir is the torn surface of the Mid-Atlantic ridge itself, and Iceland's Althing met under its cliffs from 930 until 1798.

clue: Where did the largest Nazi death camp imprison and murder more than a million people?
fact: Auschwitz-Birkenau's electrified fences and guard towers stand on the site, and the camp's own railway siding was laid by prisoners forced to build it.

clue: Where did the 1986 explosion of a nuclear reactor require a giant steel coffin over the ruins?
fact: In 2016 a 25,000-tonne sarcophagus was slid across Chernobyl's destroyed fourth reactor in a single 36-hour operation.

clue: Where were medieval kings crowned on the stone that Edward I carried off to Westminster Abbey in 1296?
fact: English undergraduates carried the Stone of Destiny off from Scone Abbey on Christmas Day 1950, and it now sits in Edinburgh Castle.

clue: Where was the largest castle in the world taken apart brick by brick and rebuilt 250 kilometres away?
fact: Malbork Castle, built by the Teutonic Knights, was dismantled and ferried across Poland to become a royal castle after the Treaty of Thorn in 1466.

clue: Where does midwinter sunlight enter a stone mound and light up a chamber built 5,000 years ago?
fact: Newgrange is aligned to the winter solstice sun, and for a few minutes each December afternoon the beam enters the roof box and strikes the back wall.

clue: Where were kings crowned in stone until 1101, on a limestone outcrop the devil supposedly cracked?
fact: Legend says St Patrick trapped the devil on the Rock of Cashel and tricked him into exempting the town from hell by cracking its roof.

clue: Where did Luther hide and translate the New Testament into German?
fact: In Wartburg Castle Martin Luther translated the New Testament from Greek in about a fortnight in 1521, and the Bible that came out of it made him a fugitive.

clue: Where does the most complete Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall sit on open moorland?
fact: Housesteads was garrisoned from about AD 122, and its turf-covered rampart still holds the silhouette of the empire's northern frontier ditch.

clue: Where does an island church with twenty-two wooden domes stand on Lake Onega?
fact: The log walls of Kizhi's Church of the Transfiguration held no nails at all, a fact confirmed only in 1990 when a rescue restoration finally let them put some in.

clue: Where was Custer's Last Stand?
fact: The Little Bighorn Battlefield marks where Lieutenant Colonel George Custer and his troops were defeated by Lakota and Cheyenne forces in 1876.

clue: Where is the modernist National Congress complex designed by Oscar Niemeyer?
fact: Oscar Niemeyer designed the paired towers and opposing bowl-shaped chambers. The complex is a defining work of modernist Brasilia.

clue: Where does an ancient Greek theatre frame views of Mount Etna and the sea from a clifftop town?
fact: Ancient theatre with Etna views.

clue: Where is Funchal’s old town, known for painted doors and a waterfront market?
fact: Historic center of Madeira.

clue: Where is the mountaintop castle above Hechingen, ancestral seat of an imperial dynasty?
fact: Around 700 years old, it survived WWII largely because its people were evacuees from Berlin, then served as the residence of the last emperor of Germany.

clue: Where is the pyramidal peak that marks the border of Switzerland and Italy?
fact: The first ascent in 1865 ended in tragedy when four climbers fell during the descent, and the mountain's name comes from its horn-like shape.

clue: Where is Germany's highest peak, on the border with Austria?
fact: At 2,962 m it is Germany's highest mountain, and two countries' boundary runs right across its summit, complete with a customs hut.

clue: Where is the lakeside Alpine village famous for its salt mine and Iron Age cemetery?
fact: Salt mined here since the Bronze Age funded the Hallstatt culture, and in 1847 an ossuary containing 6,000 skulls was uncovered beneath the chapel.

clue: Where is the colourful fishing village perched on a cliff in the Cinque Terre?
fact: Its tiny harbour, reached only by a 353-step stairway, has been worked by generations of Genoese fishermen, and the village appears on Italian banknotes.

clue: Where is the castle whose turrets are modelled on an inverted ship's hull?
fact: Begun in the 12th century and never finished, its slate spires were reputedly shaped to resemble the hulls of Castilian galleons.

clue: Where is the semicircular plaza decorated with tiled alcoves for each of the country's provinces?
fact: Built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition, its alcoves were nicknamed seating alcoves because young men used them to talk to their girlfriends.

clue: Where is Madrid's museum holding Las Meninas and Goya's black paintings?
fact: Called the Prado after an oak grove that once stood on the site, it opened in 1819 and holds some 8,600 paintings.

clue: Where is the pilgrimage cathedral whose botafumeiro swings beneath its crossing?
fact: The Botafumeiro censer swings through the transept from eight people, and the square is said to be where the apostle was beheaded.

clue: Where is the Roman spa complex beside the River Avon?
fact: Hot water from the same spring still fills the Great Bath, and the site lends the English city of Bath its name.

clue: Where is the walled Adriatic old town climbing the slopes of a fjord-like bay?
fact: Its defensive walls climb almost 1,200 m to the fortress of San Giovanni, and the bay was one of the Mediterranean's busiest medieval ports.

clue: Where is the castle whose interiors feature trompe-l’oeil landscapes above a bend in the Vltava?
fact: Its Baroque theatre is one of the few still working today, and the town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

clue: Where is the glacial boulder wedged above a deep fjord at Kjerag?
fact: People pose at the edge of a 984 m drop under the stone, which broke from the mountain in an Ice Age landslide and landed there by chance.

clue: Where is the rock tongue jutting out over a mountain lake?
fact: A cliff formed when a glacier's rockfall hit the valley wall, the tongue's name comes from trolls supposedly using it as a lookout.

clue: Where is the rocky promontory at the southwestern tip of the Cape Peninsula?
fact: Its cliffs mark the boundary between the Atlantic and Indian oceans, though the actual meeting point lies further east at Cape Agulhas.

clue: Where is the wooded island in the Okavango Delta reachable only by dugout canoe?
fact: Some 700 large animals and many bird species live here, and the island is considered the delta's most biodiverse spot.

clue: Where is the shallow Rift Valley lake famous for its tree-climbing lions?
fact: Its groundwater springs support huge flocks of flamingos, and the surrounding forest is home to both baboons and hundreds of tree-climbing lions.

clue: Where is the wildlife park near Lake Naivasha named after a gorge with fierce hot springs?
fact: Geologists came here in 1840 expecting to find traces of hell, and the park is one of the few places where visitors walk among giraffes on foot.

clue: Where are the towering red dunes of the Namib Desert with white gypsum dead trees?
fact: Some dunes here reach 300 m, and the Tsauchab river only reaches the pan a few times a century after heavy rains.

clue: Where is Africa's largest canyon, a 160 km gorge in Namibia?
fact: It drops over 500 m into the Ai-Ais Richtersveld, and ancient hominid footprints have been found on its floor.

clue: Where is the British slaving fort on the old Gold Coast?
fact: It held thousands of captives awaiting ships in the Atlantic trade, and one gate bears the inscription 'I hope you will remember my suffering.'

clue: Where is the active volcano on an island in the Indian Ocean?
fact: One of the most active volcanoes on Earth, it has produced more than 150 recorded eruptions, most recently adding hectares of new land.

clue: Where is the oldest Buddhist temple in Japan's capital, at the heart of Asakusa?
fact: Legend says a fisherman found a statue in the Sumida River in 628 AD, and its lantern is the emblem of Asakusa.

clue: Where is the Kyoto Zen temple wrapped in gold leaf on a pond?
fact: The pavilion was burned down by a teenage monk in 1950 and rebuilt three years later, and the name means golden turtle because of its lake setting.

clue: Where is the white 'egret' castle rising over a city, with complex fireproof roofs?
fact: Its stepped gables hide the rooms from outside, and its curved walls of white plaster earned it the name White Heron Castle.

clue: Where is the Shinto shrine whose great torii gate appears to stand in the sea?
fact: At high tide the 16 m gate stands in open water on tidal flats, and the shrine has been rebuilt many times, most recently 1875.

clue: Where is the Ryukyu royal palace in Okinawa, rebuilt after war?
fact: Its pillar tombs preserved the bones of visiting envoys, and the castle was destroyed in the 1945 Battle of Okinawa before being reconstructed in the 1990s.

clue: Where is the Silla-era Buddhist temple paired with the Seokguram grotto near Gyeongju?
fact: It was completed in 751 CE and its wooden halls survived Japanese occupation because they sat on a hill above the city.

clue: Where is the best-preserved Ming-dynasty section of the Great Wall, with watchtowers?
fact: Roughly 5,400 m of wall survives here, and sliding doorways let guards block enemy access along the ramparts.

clue: Where is the walled Ming-dynasty city where the Rishengchang draft bank was founded?
fact: Its 6 km wall was never taken by an enemy, and the Rishengchang draft bank operated there for over 400 years.

clue: Where are the twin stainless steel towers in Kuala Lumpur joined by a skybridge?
fact: Standing 452 m tall, they were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004, and the towers' floor plan is an eight-pointed Islamic star.

clue: Where is the smoking volcano inside the Tengger caldera on Java?
fact: Hindus hold a yearly Kasada ceremony offering livestock in exchange for good harvests, and the volcano's name comes from Brahma.

clue: Where are the 1,268 grassy mounds in Bohol that look like spilled chocolate?
fact: The cones grew as coral limestone lifted during earthquakes, and the name was coined by a film crew filming a 2012 ad.

clue: Where is the near-perfect cone erupting on the island of Luzon?
fact: Its slopes are almost perfectly 45 degrees, and around 47 eruptions are recorded, making it one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines.

clue: Where is the cave system holding the world's longest river cave?
fact: Son Doong, the largest cave passage in the world, lies within the reserve, and Sơn Đoòng has its own jungle and weather system.

clue: Where is the old trading port with hundreds of yellow merchant houses?
fact: It was a major port from the 1500s to the 1800s and its Japanese Covered Bridge dates to the 16th century.

clue: Where is the monastery clinging to a cliff 900 m above the Paro valley?
fact: The building appears to be on the cliff face with no visible support, and the walls inside are decorated with painted tiger claws.

clue: Where is the temple built as a giant stone chariot for the sun god?
fact: Its 24 giant wheels are carved with scenes, and the tower stands where the roof once served as a sundial.

clue: Where is the Abu Dhabi mosque with white domes and 96 columns inlaid with mother-of-pearl?
fact: It can hold over 40,000 worshippers including 9,200 seated under its main dome, which is clad in 1,000 domes.

clue: Where is the Mughal mosque in Lahore, once the largest in the world?
fact: The 1673 mosque holds 100,000 worshippers, and its four minarets are faced in red sandstone with marble inlay.

clue: Where are the sandstone buttes rising from the Arizona desert floor?
fact: The valley's walls are volcanic ash left by ancient eruptions, and the Navajo name Tsegi'ani'i means the land of the tall pines.

clue: Where is the Utah amphitheatre filled with orange hoodoos spires?
fact: The park sits at 2,400-2,700 m, and its rock formed when a lake bottom was lifted and eroded.

clue: Where is the glacial California valley beneath El Capitan and Half Dome?
fact: A glacial river carved the valley during the last ice age, and the first Yosemite National Park in the world was dedicated here in 1890.

clue: Where is the New York suspension bridge opened in 1883?
fact: Its hybrid cable design was once thought too daring, and its main cables each contain 5,434 parallel steel wires.

clue: Where is the Florida launch site for NASA crewed missions?
fact: Launch pad 39A has sent every crewed moon mission to space, and its 120 m Saturn V still stands as a monument.

clue: Where is the lowest point in North America, 86 m below sea level?
fact: At 120 m long and 1.6 km wide, it holds temporary lakes and salt flats after rare rains, and salt polygons form as the water evaporates.

clue: Where is the 1,780-square-km peat swamp of Georgia and Florida, from a Choctaw name meaning bubble water?
fact: Long called the land of the dancing bears, it sits only 33 m above sea level and hosts dense black bear and wild boar populations.

clue: Where is the grand hotel above the Terrasse Dufferin in Quebec City?
fact: Commissioned by the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1893, it sits on the site of a 23rd-century chateau built by French governor Charles de Frontenac.

clue: Where is the city of pyramids whose name means the place where the gods were made?
fact: It was the largest city in the Americas for centuries, then was burned and abandoned, and no records of its builders survive.

clue: Where is the vast network of copper-green canyons crossed by the railway known as El Chepe?
fact: Cheyenne and Tarahumara Indians live in the canyons, and the ridged terrain comes from copper-impregnated rock staining blue-green.

clue: Where is the Maya temple complex rising above the Petén rainforest?
fact: Its Temple IV is 65 m tall, the tallest Maya structure ever built, and its lost twin pyramid was found by archaeologists in 2015 using ground-penetrating radar.

clue: Where are the twin volcanic peaks and emerald crater lake in the Caribbean?
fact: The Pitons rise over 2,500 m from the sea, and the island's Pitons are drawn on its flag and national football badge.

clue: Where are the shifting white dunes and freshwater lagoons near the equatorial Atlantic coast?
fact: Local fishermen say the town is blessed by Saint Jericho, and the dunes migrate westward with the trade winds.

clue: Where are the white sand dunes and blue freshwater lagoons of Maranhão?
fact: Rainwater pools between the dunes for months, creating islands of sand and fishing lakes of pure fresh water.

clue: Where is the archaeological site reached by a four-day trek through the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta?
fact: The Tairona built it on a ridge in the 12th-16th centuries, and it was lost to outsiders for four centuries before being rediscovered in 1972.

clue: Where is the white-sand beach with palm groves and moai on Easter Island?
fact: Anakena was the island's only sandy beach, and the moai facing inland are thought to mark the burial site of the first arriving king.

clue: Where is the tropical park with sandstone escarpments, ancient rock art and monsoon wetlands?
fact: Its name is a mis-spelling of the region's Aboriginal name, and it holds more than 1,400 documented archaeological sites.

clue: Where are the three sandstone peaks above the Blue Mountains west of Sydney?
fact: Erosion along a fault formed them, and the area was painted by Aboriginal artists thousands of years ago as the Three Sisters.

clue: Where is the highest mountain in Australia?
fact: At 2,228 m it is a glaciated eroded peak in the Australian Alps, and skiers race down its run each August.

clue: Where is the turquoise glacial lake on South Island, famed for its dark skies and lakeside chapel?
fact: The blue colour comes from rock flour ground by glaciers suspended in the water, and the region is a Dark Sky Reserve.

clue: Where is the cave system where thousands of glowworms illuminate underground boat passages?
fact: Its ceiling is dotted with around 50,000 glowworm larvae, which use sticky mucus threads and lower threads to catch flying insects.

clue: Where did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin after noticing bacteria would not grow near a mold?
fact: Fleming made the observation in 1928 in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital. The room has since been reconstructed as the Alexander Fleming Laboratory Museum.

clue: Where did Watson and Crick build the double-helix model of DNA in 1953?
fact: The breakthrough was made at Cambridge University's old Cavendish Laboratory, aided by crucial X-ray evidence produced by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.

clue: Where did Enrico Fermi's team produce the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction?
fact: Chicago Pile-1 went critical beneath the stands of the University of Chicago's Stagg Field on December 2, 1942. Henry Moore's sculpture now marks the site.

clue: Where was the first working transistor demonstrated in 1947?
fact: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley's group developed the device at Bell Telephone Laboratories, launching the solid-state electronics era.

clue: Where did scientists announce evidence of the long-sought Higgs boson in 2012?
fact: The ATLAS and CMS teams at CERN jointly reported a new Higgs-like particle. This point marks the ATLAS detector site on the Large Hadron Collider ring.

clue: Where was the first direct detection of gravitational waves made as twin detectors registered colliding black holes?
fact: LIGO's Hanford and Livingston observatories detected the same signal on September 14, 2015. Hanford's immense L-shaped interferometer is one of the two discovery sites.

clue: Where did Ernest Rutherford's team first split the atomic nucleus in 1917?
fact: At the University of Manchester, Rutherford bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles and identified emitted hydrogen nuclei, the first artificial transmutation of an element.

clue: Where did Jocelyn Bell Burnell first detect the repeating radio signals of a pulsar?
fact: In 1967 Bell Burnell spotted the signal in chart-recorder data from Cambridge's Interplanetary Scintillation Array. The source was briefly nicknamed LGM-1 before being recognized as a neutron star.

clue: Where was Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell, created?
fact: Dolly was born at the Roslin Institute in 1996 after scientists transferred a nucleus from an adult sheep cell into an egg cell.

clue: Where did Christiaan Barnard perform the first human-to-human heart transplant?
fact: The operation took place on December 3, 1967, at Cape Town's Groote Schuur Hospital. Its original operating theatres are preserved as the Heart of Cape Town Museum.

clue: Where did the Wright brothers make the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered airplane?
fact: Orville flew the Flyer for 12 seconds on December 17, 1903, from level ground beside Kill Devil Hill. A marker shows where that first flight ended.

clue: Where did Alexander Graham Bell make the first intelligible telephone call, asking Watson to come to him?
fact: Bell spoke the famous request in his Boston laboratory on March 10, 1876. The original building is gone, but a plaque near the site records the call.

clue: Where did Thomas Edison's team demonstrate a long-lasting practical incandescent lamp in 1879?
fact: Edison's Menlo Park laboratory became known as an invention factory. A memorial tower and museum stand where the research complex operated.

clue: Where did the Lumière brothers stage the first commercial public film screening in 1895?
fact: Paying spectators watched ten short films in the basement Salon Indien on Boulevard des Capucines. The site is now occupied by Hôtel Scribe Paris Opéra.

clue: Where was the first ARPANET message sent before the system crashed after the letters 'LO'?
fact: A UCLA team tried to send LOGIN to Stanford on October 29, 1969. The network failed after two letters, making 'LO' the internet ancestor's first message.

clue: Where was a product with a UPC barcode scanned at a checkout for the first time?
fact: A pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum was scanned at 8:01 a.m. on June 26, 1974, at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio.

clue: Where was the world's first cash machine opened for public use in 1967?
fact: Actor Reg Varney withdrew the first cash from the Barclays branch in Enfield. The early machine used special vouchers rather than plastic bank cards.

clue: Where did Nicéphore Niépce create the oldest surviving photograph made with a camera?
fact: Around 1826 or 1827, Niépce exposed a pewter plate for hours through an upstairs window at his estate, producing View from the Window at Le Gras.

clue: Where was the world's first traffic signal installed in 1868?
fact: The gas-lit semaphore stood outside the Houses of Parliament. It operated for only weeks before a gas leak caused an explosion that injured its police operator.

clue: Where did the 1969 Woodstock festival actually take place after its original venue plans collapsed?
fact: About 400,000 people gathered on Max Yasgur's dairy farm near Bethel, roughly 40 miles from Woodstock itself. The hillside is now part of Bethel Woods Center for the Arts.

clue: Where did the Beatles play their final public performance on a rooftop?
fact: The unannounced January 1969 concert atop Apple Corps headquarters drew crowds into the street before police brought it to an end.

clue: Where was the famous photograph of eleven ironworkers eating lunch on a steel beam high above Manhattan taken?
fact: Lunch Atop a Skyscraper was staged during construction of 30 Rockefeller Plaza in 1932. The men were genuinely sitting hundreds of feet above the street.

clue: Where did an unidentified man stand in front of a column of tanks after the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown?
fact: The confrontation occurred on Chang'an Avenue near the Beijing Hotel, just east of Tiananmen Square. Photographers in the hotel recorded the scene from above.

clue: Where was Joe Rosenthal's iconic photograph of U.S. Marines raising a flag during World War II taken?
fact: The Pulitzer-winning image captured the second flag raising on Mount Suribachi on February 23, 1945, during the Battle of Iwo Jima.

clue: Where did Dorothea Lange photograph the woman who became known as Migrant Mother?
fact: Lange met Florence Owens Thompson at a pea-pickers' camp in Nipomo in 1936. The photograph became an enduring image of the Great Depression.

clue: Where were the interior scenes of Luke Skywalker's childhood home filmed for Star Wars?
fact: A traditional underground Berber dwelling in Matmata became the Lars homestead dining room. Its Star Wars decorations have been restored for visitors.

clue: Where were many of the harbor scenes for Jaws filmed, standing in for fictional Amity Island?
fact: Steven Spielberg used Martha's Vineyard locations throughout the 1975 film. Menemsha's working harbor appeared as the movie's Amity waterfront.

clue: Where were the Shire scenes for The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit trilogies filmed?
fact: Peter Jackson chose the Alexander family's sheep farm near Matamata for its rolling green landscape. The rebuilt set was made permanent after The Hobbit films.

clue: Where did Jimi Hendrix set his guitar on fire during the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival?
fact: Hendrix's dramatic finale helped turn his U.S. festival debut into rock history. The same festival also introduced major audiences to Janis Joplin and the Who.

clue: Where was the first wooden figure burned at the gathering that evolved into Burning Man?
fact: Larry Harvey and friends burned an eight-foot wooden man on Baker Beach in 1986. The event later moved to Nevada's Black Rock Desert.

clue: Where was the epicenter of the most powerful earthquake ever instrumentally recorded?
fact: The magnitude 9.5 Great Chilean earthquake struck offshore near Valdivia on May 22, 1960. Its tsunami crossed the Pacific and caused deaths as far away as Hawaii and Japan.

clue: Where did the 1883 volcanic eruption produce an explosion heard thousands of kilometers away?
fact: Krakatau's climactic blasts collapsed much of the island and generated deadly tsunamis. Pressure waves circled the globe multiple times.

clue: Where did the 1815 eruption that caused the 'Year Without a Summer' occur?
fact: Tambora's eruption was the largest in recorded history by erupted volume. Aerosols cooled the climate and contributed to crop failures across the Northern Hemisphere.

clue: Where did a 1980 landslide uncork a devastating sideways volcanic blast?
fact: A magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered the collapse of the volcano's north flank on May 18, 1980. The lateral blast killed 57 people and flattened vast forests.

clue: Where did an exploding space rock flatten about 2,000 square kilometers of taiga forest in 1908?
fact: The Tunguska object burst in the atmosphere without leaving a conventional impact crater. The remote site was not scientifically surveyed until nearly two decades later.

clue: Where did a meteor airburst in 2013 shatter windows and injure more than a thousand people?
fact: The asteroid exploded high over Chelyabinsk Oblast, releasing far more energy than the Hiroshima bomb. Most injuries came from flying glass after the shock wave arrived.

clue: Where did a 1958 rockslide produce the highest tsunami run-up ever recorded?
fact: An earthquake sent rock plunging into the narrow Alaskan bay, stripping trees up to 524 meters above sea level. Two people in fishing boats were killed.

clue: Where did the enormous 2022 submarine eruption send pressure waves around the world?
fact: The eruption generated a towering plume, a Pacific-wide tsunami, and atmospheric waves detected globally. Much of the young volcanic island was destroyed.

clue: Where did volcanic mudflows bury a town and kill more than 20,000 people in 1985?
fact: A relatively small eruption of Nevado del Ruiz melted summit ice, sending lahars down river valleys into Armero. The catastrophe became a stark lesson in ignored volcanic warnings.

clue: Where did an iron asteroid leave one of Earth's best-preserved impact craters about 50,000 years ago?
fact: The Arizona crater is about 1.2 kilometers wide. Daniel Barringer's unsuccessful search for a huge buried meteor helped establish its impact origin.

clue: Where did nine hikers mysteriously abandon their tent and die in the Ural Mountains in 1959?
fact: Searchers found the tent cut open from inside on the slope of Kholat Syakhl. A later Russian inquiry concluded that a slab avalanche was the most likely trigger.

clue: Where did English settlers vanish, leaving only the word 'CROATOAN' carved at their abandoned colony?
fact: When John White returned in 1590, he found the Roanoke settlement dismantled and its inhabitants gone. Their ultimate fate remains uncertain.

clue: Where did three lighthouse keepers disappear without explanation in December 1900?
fact: A relief crew reached Eilean Mòr to find the lighthouse deserted. Investigators suspected a huge wave swept the keepers away, but no bodies were recovered.

clue: Where were six residents of an isolated farm murdered in an enduring 1922 mystery?
fact: The killer apparently remained at Hinterkaifeck for days, feeding livestock and using the kitchen. The farm was demolished the following year and the crime remains unsolved.

clue: Where was the unidentified 'Isdal Woman' found dead in 1970 with labels removed from her belongings?
fact: Hikers found the burned body in a remote valley near Bergen. False identities, coded notes, and unexplained travels have fueled decades of speculation.

clue: Where did the Zodiac killer attack two students beside a lake while wearing a hooded costume?
fact: The September 1969 attack occurred at a secluded shoreline spot on Lake Berryessa. A message on the victims' car door linked it to earlier shootings.

clue: Where did the United States defeat the Soviet Union in the 1980 'Miracle on Ice'?
fact: The U.S. hockey team upset the heavily favored Soviets 4–3 at the Lake Placid Winter Olympics, then beat Finland to win gold.

clue: Where did Diego Maradona score both the 'Hand of God' and the 'Goal of the Century' in one World Cup match?
fact: Maradona's contrasting goals carried Argentina past England in the 1986 quarter-final. Argentina went on to win the tournament.

clue: Where did Muhammad Ali use the rope-a-dope to defeat George Foreman in the 'Rumble in the Jungle'?
fact: Ali knocked out the previously unbeaten champion in Kinshasa in 1974. The bout began before dawn so it could air during U.S. prime time.

clue: Where did Roger Bannister run the first sub-four-minute mile?
fact: Bannister ran 3:59.4 on May 6, 1954, paced by Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway at Oxford University's track.

clue: Where did Bob Beamon make his astonishing 8.90-meter long jump at the 1968 Olympics?
fact: Beamon exceeded the existing world record by 55 centimeters, forcing officials to use a steel tape because the optical measuring device could not reach the mark.

clue: Where did Secretariat win by 31 lengths to complete the 1973 Triple Crown?
fact: Secretariat's 2:24 Belmont Stakes remains the fastest 1.5 miles on dirt in racing history. His immense margin produced one of sport's defining photographs.

clue: Where was the ceremonial golden spike driven to complete the first transcontinental railroad in the United States?
fact: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads met at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869. A telegraphed signal let the nation follow the final blows in real time.

clue: Where did Yuri Gagarin launch to become the first human in space?
fact: Vostok 1 lifted off from Baikonur's Site No. 1 on April 12, 1961. The pad became known as Gagarin's Start.

clue: Where did the first nonstop transatlantic airplane flight land in 1919?
fact: John Alcock and Arthur Brown mistook an Irish bog near Clifden for a firm field and nosed over on landing. Both men walked away after flying from Newfoundland.

clue: Where did Charles Lindbergh land after making the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight?
fact: Lindbergh reached Le Bourget after 33.5 hours in the Spirit of St. Louis on May 21, 1927. A huge crowd rushed onto the airfield to meet him.

clue: Where were peaceful voting-rights marchers attacked by law officers on Bloody Sunday in 1965?
fact: State troopers and a sheriff's posse assaulted marchers just after they crossed the bridge in Selma. Televised images helped build support for the Voting Rights Act.

clue: Where did King John seal Magna Carta in 1215?
fact: King John met rebel barons in the meadow beside the Thames at Runnymede. The charter became a lasting symbol of limits on arbitrary power.

clue: Where was Abraham Lincoln shot while watching Our American Cousin?
fact: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln in the presidential box on April 14, 1865, then escaped by leaping to the stage. Lincoln died the next morning across the street.

clue: Where was President John F. Kennedy assassinated during a motorcade in 1963?
fact: Kennedy was fatally shot as his limousine passed through Dealey Plaza. The former Texas School Book Depository now houses a museum about the assassination.

clue: Where was Martin Luther King Jr. assassinated in 1968?
fact: King was shot while standing on the motel's second-floor balcony in Memphis. The preserved Lorraine Motel is now part of the National Civil Rights Museum.

clue: Where was Mahatma Gandhi assassinated while walking to an evening prayer meeting?
fact: Nathuram Godse shot Gandhi in the grounds of Birla House on January 30, 1948. Stone footprints trace Gandhi's final walk through the garden.

clue: Where was Archduke Franz Ferdinand assassinated in the event that helped trigger World War I?
fact: Gavrilo Princip shot the archduke and Sophie beside Sarajevo's Latin Bridge on June 28, 1914, after an earlier bomb attempt failed.

clue: Where did the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire kill 146 garment workers?
fact: Many workers could not escape the upper floors of the Manhattan factory because an exit door was locked. The disaster accelerated workplace safety reforms.

clue: Where did a toxic gas leak cause one of history's deadliest industrial disasters in 1984?
fact: Methyl isocyanate escaped from a Union Carbide pesticide plant and drifted over nearby neighborhoods. Thousands died and survivors continue to suffer health effects.

clue: Where did the Hindenburg airship catch fire while attempting to land in 1937?
fact: The zeppelin burned at Lakehurst Naval Air Station in 34 seconds, killing 35 aboard and one ground worker. Newsreel footage helped end the passenger-airship era.

clue: Where did two ships collide in 1917, causing the largest human-made explosion before the atomic age?
fact: The munitions ship Mont-Blanc exploded after colliding with Imo in Halifax Harbour. The blast devastated Richmond and killed nearly 2,000 people.

clue: Where did a 1969 police raid spark days of resistance that became a landmark in the LGBTQ rights movement?
fact: Patrons and neighbors resisted a routine raid at the Stonewall Inn in Greenwich Village. Annual Pride marches grew from commemorations held one year later.

clue: Where did border guards first open a checkpoint to crowds on November 9, 1989?
fact: Under mounting pressure and without clear orders, the Bornholmer Straße guards raised the barrier. It became the first border crossing breached that night.

clue: Where did a police raid capture anti-apartheid leaders whose trial sent Nelson Mandela to prison for life?
fact: Security police raided the secret African National Congress meeting place in Rivonia in 1963. Documents seized there became key evidence in the Rivonia Trial.

clue: Where were members of Israel's Olympic team taken hostage during the 1972 Summer Games?
fact: Black September gunmen entered the Israeli team's residence in the Olympic Village. The crisis ultimately left eleven Israeli team members and a West German police officer dead.

clue: Where did Muhammad Ali light the Olympic cauldron in a surprise appearance at the 1996 opening ceremony?
fact: Ali's visibly trembling hands made the moment especially powerful. The cauldron structure survives near the site of the former Centennial Olympic Stadium.

clue: Where did Martin Luther King Jr. deliver his 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
fact: King addressed the March on Washington from the Lincoln Memorial steps before an estimated 250,000 people. An inscription marks where he stood.

clue: Where was the first Academy Awards ceremony held in 1929?
fact: The inaugural Oscars were presented during a private dinner in the hotel's Blossom Room. The ceremony lasted only about fifteen minutes.

clue: Where did Elvis Presley record 'That's All Right,' the single that launched his career?
fact: During a break in a 1954 session, Presley began playing Arthur Crudup's song and producer Sam Phillips recognized the sound he wanted.

clue: Where did thousands gather to launch the Montgomery bus boycott and endorse Martin Luther King Jr. as its leader?
fact: On December 5, 1955, an overflowing mass meeting voted to continue the one-day boycott. The protest lasted more than a year and ended segregated city buses.

clue: Where did Captain Matthew Webb come ashore after the first recorded unaided swim across the English Channel?
fact: Webb swam from Dover to the Calais coast in nearly 22 hours in 1875, battling currents and jellyfish without a wetsuit.

clue: Where does this stone bridge thread through the sandstone pinnacles of Saxon Switzerland above the Elbe River?
fact: The present sandstone bridge was completed in 1851, replacing an earlier wooden crossing between the Bastei rock formations.

clue: Which fortified village of earthen towers stands beside the Ounila River on the old caravan route to Marrakesh?
fact: This UNESCO-listed ksar is a compact group of earthen buildings enclosed by defensive walls and corner towers.

clue: Which vast square fort, ringed by forty round bastions, rises from the Cholistan Desert?
fact: Derawar's forty bastions form walls roughly 1.5 kilometres around and can be seen from far across the desert.

clue: Where is this mountaintop walled settlement built by the Chachapoya people in the northern Andes?
fact: Kuélap's massive limestone walls enclose hundreds of structures at about 3,000 metres above sea level.

clue: Which Nabataean archaeological site contains monumental tombs carved into isolated sandstone outcrops?
fact: Hegra was the Nabataeans' major southern city and became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

clue: Which citadel overlooks a UNESCO-listed city nicknamed the City of Stone for its slate-roofed Ottoman houses?
fact: The fortress dominates the Drino valley and today contains a military museum and the stage for Gjirokastër's folk festival.

clue: Where is this otherworldly hydrothermal field of sulphur, salt and vivid mineral pools in the Danakil Depression?
fact: Dallol lies below sea level, where geothermal brines create intensely coloured salt formations in one of Earth's hottest regions.

clue: Where is the Inca complex famous for zigzag walls assembled from enormous, tightly fitted stones?
fact: Some blocks in Sacsayhuamán's three terraced walls weigh well over 100 tonnes, yet were fitted without mortar.

clue: Which geometric stepwell in Rajasthan descends through thousands of symmetrical steps at the village of Abhaneri?
fact: Built around the 8th or 9th century, Chand Baori has 13 levels and roughly 3,500 narrow steps.

clue: Which Renaissance castle is built directly into the mouth of a cave beneath a towering limestone cliff?
fact: A network of passages behind Predjama Castle links it to the cave system and once provided a concealed supply route.

clue: Which colossal temple at Ellora was carved downward from a single mass of basalt?
fact: Kailasa is Cave 16 at Ellora; builders excavated the freestanding temple from the top down rather than assembling it stone by stone.

clue: Which three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge crosses the Gardon River near Nîmes in southern France?
fact: The bridge carried the Nîmes aqueduct across the valley and survives as the tallest Roman aqueduct bridge still standing.

clue: Which abandoned saucer-shaped communist monument crowns Hadzhi Dimitar Peak?
fact: Opened in 1981 as a memorial house for the Bulgarian Communist Party, the concrete monument was abandoned after the regime fell.

clue: Which red-brick Gothic castle occupies an island in Lake Galvė, west of a Baltic capital?
fact: Completed around 1409, the restored island fortress was an important residence of the rulers of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

clue: Where do centuries-old Orthodox monasteries perch atop immense sandstone pillars above Thessaly?
fact: Meteora's monastic community began forming in the 14th century; six of its dramatically situated monasteries remain active today.

clue: Where do thousands of narrow quartz-sandstone pillars rise through mist-covered forest in Hunan?
fact: Zhangjiajie National Forest Park forms part of the Wulingyuan scenic area, whose eroded stone pillars can rise hundreds of metres above the valleys.

clue: Which vast whitewashed fortress stands between two converging rivers, with jacaranda trees framing its tiered courtyards?
fact: Built in 1637–38, this dzong remains both a monastic center and an administrative seat.

clue: Which restored stone castle occupies a tiny tidal island where three sea lochs meet?
fact: The medieval stronghold was destroyed in 1719 and reconstructed in the early twentieth century.

clue: Which futuristic monument links nine giant metal spheres into the form of a magnified iron crystal?
fact: Built for the 1958 World's Fair, the 102-metre structure represents a unit cell enlarged 165 billion times.

clue: Which medieval cave monastery forms hundreds of chambers across the face of a river-valley cliff?
fact: Its principal construction dates to the twelfth century, and the complex once extended across as many as nineteen tiers.

clue: Which ruined fortress crowns a sheer-sided coastal headland reached by a narrow path and steep steps?
fact: Its secluded position helped safeguard the Scottish crown jewels from invading forces in the seventeenth century.

clue: Which white coastal fortress began as a fifteenth-century trading post and later became bound to the transatlantic slave trade?
fact: Erected in 1482, it is the oldest surviving European-built structure south of the Sahara.

short: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace
clue: Which monumental domed basilica rises from a planned inland capital, surrounded by a vast paved esplanade?
fact: Completed in 1989, the complex covers about 30,000 square metres and its dome rises to 158 metres.

clue: Which intricately carved stepwell descends through seven levels like an inverted temple dedicated to water?
fact: The eleventh-century structure contains more than 500 principal sculptures and was rediscovered after centuries beneath silt.

clue: Which ninth-century monastery sits on a basalt plateau above a deep gorge, once reached by a long aerial tramway?
fact: The complex was a major medieval center of learning and housed a university in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

clue: Which royal burial compound is centered on a huge circular thatched building made with reeds, wood, and earth?
fact: The site contains the tombs of four kings and is a major spiritual center for the Baganda people.

clue: Which underground church occupies chambers carved into a former halite mine, with illuminated crosses cut from dark rock?
fact: The current sanctuary opened in 1995 about 200 metres below ground and has three principal naves.

clue: Which enormous early nineteenth-century fortress dominates a mountaintop, its battery walls overlooking the northern plain?
fact: Tens of thousands of workers built the stronghold after independence as protection against a feared invasion.

clue: Which remarkably preserved colonial citadel climbs a steep volcanic hill above a narrow Caribbean coastline?
fact: British military engineers designed the fortifications, which were constructed and maintained largely by enslaved Africans.

clue: Which roofless medieval cathedral stands amid grassland ruins near a deeply cut border ravine?
fact: Completed around the start of the eleventh century, it was designed by the architect Trdat.

clue: Which small whitewashed adobe mosque is bristled with timber supports and pyramidal buttresses?
fact: Repeated community restoration has preserved one of West Africa's oldest surviving mosques and its earthen-building traditions.

clue: Which tiny hermitage crowns a narrow limestone monolith roughly forty metres above the surrounding woodland?
fact: Religious buildings have occupied the pillar since at least the early medieval period; modern access is by a metal ladder.

clue: Which sprawling temple complex has moat-bound ruins, long narrative reliefs, and towers bearing serene stone faces?
fact: Built in the late twelfth or early thirteenth century, its reliefs include rare scenes of historic battles and daily life.

clue: Which abandoned royal center is recognized by patterned dry-stone terrace walls built across a wooded hillside?
fact: The settlement flourished after the fifteenth century, and its decorated retaining walls supported elite compounds.

clue: Which pre-Hispanic settlement spreads as low stone foundations and reconstructed walls across an arid mountain slope?
fact: The fortified community resisted outside rule for centuries before its inhabitants were forcibly displaced in 1667.

clue: Which Shandong ceramics center gave its name to Zibo barbecue’s distinctive pancakes, scallions, and tabletop grills?
fact: Zibo was the capital of the ancient state of Qi and became a viral food destination in 2023 for its DIY barbecue.

clue: Which Ganges city once called the “Manchester of the East” is associated with leather works and IIT Kanpur?
fact: Kanpur is an industrial city on the Ganges that became India's leather capital and was a key site of the 1857 uprising.

clue: Which Japanese manufacturing center is home to Nagoya Castle, Atsuta Shrine, and Toyota’s industrial roots?
fact: Nagoya is the hub of Japan's car industry, with Toyota headquartered nearby, and is known for its golden-dolphin castle.

clue: Which northern Nigerian city was designed as a colonial administrative center and hosts the colorful Kaduna polo tournament?
fact: Kaduna is a northern Nigerian city that served as the capital of the colonial Northern Region and is a textile and military center.

clue: Which southern Turkish city is famed for the Roman stone bridge, Sabancı Mosque, and spicy Adana kebab?
fact: Adana is a Turkish city on the Seyhan River, famous for its spicy minced-meat Adana kebab.

clue: Which ancient Ganges capital is associated with Pataliputra, Ashoka, and the enormous Sikh shrine Takht Sri Patna Sahib?
fact: Patna, ancient Pataliputra, was the capital of the Maurya Empire and sits on the south bank of the Ganges.

clue: Which Hunan city beside Dongting Lake is associated with poet Qu Yuan and spicy Changde rice noodles?
fact: Changde is a Hunan city on the Yuan River, known for its long poetry wall along the river embankment.

clue: Which Mughal city on the Yamuna is home to the white-marble Taj Mahal and the massive red-sandstone Agra Fort?
fact: Agra is home to the Taj Mahal, built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

clue: Which capital stretches between Lake Managua and the Tiscapa...
fact: Managua is Nicaragua's capital on the shore of Lake Xolotlán, rebuilt after a devastating 1972 earthquake.

clue: Which dense municipality west of São Paulo is known for its enormous retail district and the striking metal Osasco Viaduct?
fact: Osasco is a city west of São Paulo, home to the headquarters of Bradesco, one of Brazil's biggest banks.

clue: Which ABC-region city grew around railways and industry and is home to the grand Museu de Santo André?
fact: Santo André is one of the 'ABC' industrial cities on the southeast edge of greater São Paulo.

clue: Which Pretoria township is known for Tswana culture and the massive Soshanguve Crossing commercial hub?
fact: Soshanguve is a large township north of Pretoria, whose name combines several South African languages.

clue: Which settlement south of Luanda lies beside the Kwanza River and the historic Calumbo church?
fact: Calumbo is a small settlement south of Luanda, on the banks of the Kwanza River.

clue: Which Kasai city is a major diamond-trading center at the confluence of the Tshikapa and Kasai rivers?
fact: Tshikapa is a DR Congo diamond-mining city where the Tshikapa River meets the Kasai River.

clue: Which Guadalajara suburb includes the Basilica of Our Lady of Zapopan and the vast Andares commercial district?
fact: Zapopan is part of greater Guadalajara and holds the Basilica of Our Lady of Zapopan and the Estadio Akron.

clue: Which bay in New Zealand's far north, dotted with over 140 islands, is where the Treaty of Waitangi was signed?
fact: More than 140 islands dot this subtropical bay, an early center of Māori-European contact and modern sailing.

clue: Which capital's skyline faces the Pacific entrance to the Panama Canal?
fact: Its skyline stands beside the Pacific entrance to the canal that transformed global shipping.

clue: Which Ontario town, where the Niagara River meets Lake Ontario, is known for wineries and the Shaw Festival?
fact: Niagara-on-the-Lake is a town in Ontario, Canada.
